sources_short: Sentinel-2 L2A (Copernicus/ESA via Microsoft Planetary Computer), ESA WorldCover 2021, OpenStreetMap, GBIF

indicators.label: Woodland nearby
indicators.how: Share of trees within 600 m (the square and its 8 neighbours).
indicators.why: Deer and boar need cover within reach to rest, hide and escape; on hot days woodland is the best shade (Biological Conservation 2025).

indicators.label: Tree cover in the square
indicators.how: Share of the 200 m square covered by trees.
indicators.why: Dense cover inside the square itself: important for wild boar resting places.

indicators.label: Open feeding land
indicators.how: Share of grassland, cropland, shrub and wetland in the square itself (60% or more → 100).
indicators.why: Roe deer feed on meadows and fields; most sightings are on open land next to woodland.

indicators.label: Green food
indicators.how: Mean Sentinel-2 NDVI of the open land within 600 m on 24 Jul 2026 (0.25 → 0, 0.75 → 100).
indicators.why: Green, growing plants are food. Only open land is used, to avoid the "dark forest looks greenest" trap.

indicators.label: Farmland nearby
indicators.how: Share of cropland in the square itself (50% or more → 100).
indicators.why: Wild boar raid maize and cereals; crops are also roe deer food.

indicators.label: Vegetation moisture
indicators.how: Mean Sentinel-2 NDMI of the vegetation in the square, scaled to the region (2nd–98th percentile).
indicators.why: Lush, unstressed vegetation is better food in summer. Rated "high" in the feasibility study.

indicators.label: Field–forest mosaic
indicators.how: Open land in the square next to woodland around it: 4 × open share × woodland share within 600 m (a 50/50 mix → 100).
indicators.why: Roe deer are animals of the mosaic: food and cover close together.

indicators.label: Forest edge length
indicators.how: Length of tree-to-open boundary within 600 m, scaled to the region.
indicators.why: Edges are where food meets cover. Rated "high" in the feasibility study.

indicators.label: Close to a forest edge
indicators.how: Distance from the square to the nearest forest edge (on the edge → 100, 400 m or more → 0).
indicators.why: Animals that feed in the open stay close to the safety of the forest edge.

indicators.label: Away from towns
indicators.how: Mean distance to built-up land (0 m → 0, 1 km or more → 100).
indicators.why: People, dogs and traffic around villages disturb wildlife; deer keep their distance.

indicators.label: Away from roads
indicators.how: Mean distance to the nearest public road (0 m → 0, 800 m or more → 100).
indicators.why: Hunting and recreation disturb deer more than wolves do (Ecology & Evolution 2026); traffic kills and scares game.

indicators.label: Water nearby
indicators.how: Distance to the nearest river, stream, lake or wetland (water in the square → 100, 400 m or more → 0).
indicators.why: Drinking; wild boar also need wet ground to wallow in.

indicators.label: Habitat distinctiveness
indicators.how: Each land-cover type gets the distinctiveness band used in England's biodiversity metric (0 to 8): tree cover 4, grass, shrub and wetland 3, cropland 2, built-up 0, water and bare ground 3. The square's area-weighted average is scaled so that 4 → 100.
indicators.why: The biodiversity net gain metric values a habitat first by its type: woodland and semi-natural land count for more than arable fields or sealed ground.
indicators.source: ESA WorldCover 2021, bands after the statutory biodiversity metric (indicative)

indicators.label: Habitat variety
indicators.how: Shannon diversity of land-cover types within 600 m (four evenly mixed types → 100).
indicators.why: More habitat types close together support more species (landscape heterogeneity).

indicators.label: Natural cover
indicators.how: Share of the square that is forest, shrub, grassland, water or wetland.
indicators.why: Semi-natural land holds more species than arable fields or towns.

indicators.label: Plant variety (spectral)
indicators.how: Spread (standard deviation) of Sentinel-2 NDVI across the vegetation in the square, scaled to the region.
indicators.why: More variety of greenness tends to mean more plant variety (spectral variation hypothesis).

roe_deer.label: Roe deer
roe_deer.description: Roe deer habitat score v1.1: weights fitted to GBIF sightings with observer-bias correction, tested with spatial cross-validation.
roe_deer.rationale: Weights fitted to 155 roe deer sightings since 2017 against 1724 sightings of other mammals made by the same kind of observers, with guardrails: woodland nearby, the field–forest mosaic and green food always count, and no indicator takes more than 30%. Open land, farmland and the mosaic are measured inside each square, so the map shows differences from one square to the next.
roe_deer.heldout: Spatial cross-validation (9 km blocks held out): AUC 0.73 against where people report other mammals, 0.53 against the whole region. The first expert guess scored 0.51.

wild_boar.label: Wild boar
wild_boar.rationale: Wild boar rest in dense cover and feed in fields at night, so woodland, dense cover and nearby farmland lead; wet ground for wallowing and distance from villages follow. Only 7 usable GBIF records exist in the region, so these literature weights cannot be tested yet.
wild_boar.description: Wild boar habitat score v1.1 (literature weights; 7 sightings, too few to test).
wild_boar.noValidation: Only 7 usable wild boar records in GBIF here: too few to test. Hunting-bag records per hunting ground would fix this.

biodiversity.label: Biodiversity potential
biodiversity.rationale: Nature only: how valuable the habitat types are (distinctiveness, as in the biodiversity net gain metric), how many types are mixed, how much is semi-natural, how varied the vegetation is, plus water and woodland. Distance from towns and roads is left out by default so the map shows the land itself; tick them under "More indicators" to add disturbance. A proxy for how much life a place can support, not a species count.
biodiversity.description: Biodiversity potential from nature indicators only: habitat distinctiveness, variety, natural cover, plant variety, water and woodland.
biodiversity.noValidation: Not yet tested in the pilot region. Analysed areas are checked live against the variety of species recorded there (GBIF). A proper test needs surveys with known effort.

method.lead: Each 200 m square gets 15 indicators, each scaled from 0 (poor) to 100 (good). A score is the weighted average of the indicators that are ticked. All inputs are free, open data; nothing is invented.
method.validation: The roe deer score is fitted and tested on real sightings: 155 GBIF records since 2017 (citizen science, location within 250 m). People report animals where people go, so the comparison is made against 1724 records of other mammals by the same kind of observers since 2017 ("target-group background"). AUC (area under the ROC curve; ROC = receiver operating characteristic) is the chance that a square with a roe deer record scores higher than a square with another mammal record: 0.5 = no better than chance, 0.7 or more = useful. Tested on 9 km blocks the fit never saw, the score reaches AUC 0.73 (0.53 against the whole region). Only records from 2017 on are used, so the test matches the Sentinel-2 era rather than decades-old observations.
limits: One clear Sentinel-2 date (24 Jul 2026). Weekly updates and each place's seasonal normal come next.
Sightings are citizen science: they show where people see roe deer, not every place deer use. Hunting-bag, camera-trap or GPS-collar data would give a stronger test.
ESA WorldCover (2021) does not separate maize from cereals, or broadleaf from conifer forest; DLR maps can replace it in Germany.
Roads and towns outside the region are not counted, so distances near the edge are slightly too large. Footpaths and forest tracks are not counted yet.
Wild boar (7 records) and biodiversity potential cannot be tested yet; their weights come from the literature.
Scores are relative to this region; a 70 here is not the same as a 70 in another region.
